title: New laws October 1, 2026: what changes for drivers in FL and MD
dek: Several states start new laws today. Here are the driving changes in Florida and Maryland, from crash reports to clearing snow off your car.
keyPoints: Florida: the damage amount that requires an immediate crash report to police rises from $500 to $2,000.
Florida drivers can ask to get license suspension notices by email.
Maryland: drivers must make reasonable efforts to clear snow and ice from their vehicles, with fines of $25 to $200 for personal vehicles.

sources.title: New Florida laws take effect Oct. 1: Here's what to know
8 New Maryland Laws Take Effect On Oct. 1, 2026: What To Know

body: October 1 is a common start date for new state laws, and several states have a batch taking effect today, including Florida, Maryland and Connecticut. If you live in or drive through Florida or Maryland, a few of the changes touch everyday driving.

In Florida, SB 488 raises the amount of property damage that requires an immediate report to law enforcement after a crash, from $500 to $2,000. The same law makes clear that decorative license plate frames are legal as long as they do not cover registration information. Another law, SB 490, lets drivers ask the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles to send license suspension notices by email.

In Maryland, drivers now have to make reasonable efforts to remove snow and ice from their vehicles. Fines range from $25 to $200 for personal vehicles and from $75 to $1,000 for commercial vehicles. A separate Maryland law changes how car dealers can present advertised prices, allowing them to say when a price reflects a manufacturer's minimum allowable price while they offer a lower dealer price.

These summaries come from local news coverage, and each law has its own details and exceptions. Your state legislature or motor vehicle agency has the official text if you need to know exactly how a rule applies to you.
If you drive in Florida and would rather get official notices by email, look for that option on the state's motor vehicle website so nothing important sits in a mailbox you rarely check.
